thesis: The history of social norms research can be read as a series of responses to inconsistent evidence about the norm–behavior relationship, each specifying more precisely which norms, perceived by whom and under what conditions, guide behavior.

p12_run3: that treated the inconsistent evidence as a reason to specify when and how norms affect behavior. Rimal and Real (2003) distinguished descriptive from injunctive norms in a model of normative influence that also included group identity and communication among group members, on the premise that norms are constructed, understood, and disseminated through communication. Lapinski and Rimal (2005) then distinguished collective norms, which operate at the level of the social system and emerge through shared interaction, from perceived norms, which are individuals’ interpretations of those codes. In the theory of normative social behavior (TNSB), Rimal and Real (2005) specified injunctive norms, outcome expectations, and group identity as moderators of the descriptive norm–behavior relationship. In its first test, these variables were directly associated with incoming students’ intentions to drink, and several of them interacted with descriptive norms, although the interaction effects were small relative to the main effects. Communication, central to the 2003 model, was not among the constructs of the TNSB, and Lapinski and Rimal (2005) noted that the theory “does not address the ways in which normative information is communicated” (p. 133). A decade later, Rimal and Lapinski (2015) re-explicated social norms, reaffirming that “at their core, norms are communication phenomena” (p. 393), and proposed that collective norms are likely one driver of perceived descriptive norms and that communication strengthens this link, a hypothesis not yet tested.
p14: Alongside this theoretical work, communication researchers brought formative research and manipulation checks to the social norms approach,⟦FN5⟧ which made perceived norms the target of designed messages. Smith et al. (2006) used social judgment theory to measure students’ latitudes of acceptance, noncommitment, and rejection for normative information, which differed in believability, and argued that a campaign built on a true norm in the latitude of noncommitment would likely be effective. Lapinski et al. (2007) manipulated perceived prevalence with messages and verified that the manipulation changed descriptive but not injunctive perceptions, a check that earlier experiments had typically not reported. In a field experiment in men’s restrooms, descriptive norm posters increased observed hand washing relative to a no-message control, but the high- and low-prevalence messages did not differ in their effects. The message effects also remained after perceived norms were controlled, which led the authors to interpret the posters as a cue to action rather than as evidence that normative content changed behavior (Lapinski et al., 2013). A meta-analysis has since indicated that norm appeals shifted perceived norms reliably, whereas their effects on behavior were small and heterogeneous (Rhodes et al., 2020). Thus, findings on the norm–behavior relationship remain mixed, and culturally based differences in the effectiveness of norm appeals (Liu & Lapinski, 2024) point to culture as one source of that variation.
open: Theories of social norms were developed largely with U.S. and European samples, and none directly accounts for cultural dynamics in normative influence (Lapinski et al., 2022). Research on cultural dynamics has studied co-cultural groups within national boundaries and compared countries (Liu et al., 2022). In the present essay, cultural dynamics refers to (a) variation in normative influence across such groups and countries and (b) the processes through which culture is expected to shape normative influence. Culture may affect how norms are conceptualized, how much weight they carry in decisions relative to other influences, and the psychosocial dynamics through which they operate (Lapinski et al., 2022). Studies have located culture in the nation, in the individual, and, least often, in the group whose norms are studied.
A: First, culture has been located in the nation. For example, the same norm appeals shifted the targeted perceptions more in a Chinese than in a U.S. student sample, as the authors had predicted from differences in tightness, institutional signals, and message interpretation (Liu & Lapinski, 2024). None of these differences was measured, and the samples also differed in survey mode. Alternatively, a cultural dimension is scored at the level of the nation, as in Gelfand et al.’s (2011) tightness–looseness scores for 33 nations. Such scores can be examined across studies, as in a post hoc analysis in which Hofstede’s dimensions did not explain variation in the descriptive–injunctive norm correlation, although U.S.-centric research dominated the corpus (Kalny et al., 2026). Both approaches locate culture at the level of the nation, whereas country and culture are incongruent under most conditions because co-cultural groups share national identities (Liu et al., 2022).
B: Second, Lapinski et al. (2007) measured cultural orientation in individuals in response to the criticism that work on individualism–collectivism makes “broad generalizations about people from different countries” (p. 135), an approach that later studies have followed (Liu & Lapinski, 2024, 2025; Yoon et al., 2024). Group orientation, the extent to which group goals prevail over individual goals, is distinct from group identity, the TNSB moderator that refers to similarity with and aspiration toward a specific referent group (Lapinski et al., 2007; Rimal & Real, 2005). Group-oriented participants held positive water conservation attitudes and intentions regardless of perceived prevalence, which was negatively associated with both among the individualistically oriented (Lapinski et al., 2007). Group orientation was directly associated with physical distancing, but the relationships between perceived norms and distancing were steeper at lower levels of group orientation (Yoon et al., 2024). It also predicted intentions to prevent food waste without moderating the effects of norm appeals (Liu & Lapinski, 2024). For behaviors that benefit the collective, then, the group-oriented have been no more, and sometimes less, dependent on normative information than the individualistically oriented. In Chinese and U.S. adults, stating sanctions explicitly added to an injunctive appeal only among people who preferred low-context communication, and higher perceived cultural tightness strengthened some effects of injunctive appeals while weakening others (Liu & Lapinski, 2025).
C_before_fn: Third, culture has been treated as the context that defines what a norm is. Liu et al. (2022) proposed a model for culturally contextualized measurement, in which measures are developed through formative work, including interviews, within a cultural group before they are tested, and applied it with ethnically Tibetan pastoralists in Western China.
C_after_fn: In interviews, explicit communication about norms arose mainly when problems or policy changes occurred, and sanctions for deviation were implied rather than stated (Lapinski et al., 2022). Injunctive norms were therefore defined without sanctions (Liu et al., 2022), a departure from definitions that make sanctions the primary difference between injunctive and descriptive norms (Lapinski & Rimal, 2005).
D: Across these approaches, the processes through which culture is expected to alter normative influence, such as the detection of implied sanctions (Liu & Lapinski, 2025) or motivations to comply (Rimal & Lapinski, 2015), have been proposed more often than tested directly. None of the studies reviewed here manipulated culture.

fn_sna: The social norms approach seeks to change behavior by changing perceptions of a behavior’s prevalence among one’s social referents (Lapinski et al., 2007), as in campus programs that report the actual prevalence of student drinking. It originated in a finding outside the assigned readings that students overestimate their peers’ drinking (Perkins & Berkowitz, 1986).

p21: The critique has been voiced by reviewers and editors, and Rimal and Lapinski (2015) themselves acknowledged that the idea that members come to understand, negotiate, and accept or reject norms through communication had not received adequate attention (see also Yanovitzky & Rimal, 2006). To the extent that the critique presumes that research is communication research only when communication among group members is directly observed, the presumption is too narrow. Norms-based interventions rest on “a central assumption about the role of communication” (Lapinski & Rimal, 2005, p. 137), and a study that manipulates features of a normative message and analyzes how recipients perceive it examines communication effects whether or not it observes conversation. The present essay therefore considers four dimensions along which communication can be centered: as a channel of normative information, as a process of interpretation, as a condition of normative influence, and as a process through which collective norms are reproduced or changed.
p23a: With respect to the first dimension, Rimal and Real (2003) included talk about drinking with friends or siblings as a central concept of their model and proposed that “communication among like-minded individuals is a principal mechanism through which norms are transmitted” (p. 199).
p23b: Mediated channels have also been studied, as formative research (Smith et al., 2006) and norm appeal experiments (Lapinski et al., 2007, 2013; Liu & Lapinski, 2024, 2025) treat the message as a channel that moves perceived norms reliably (Rhodes et al., 2020).
p24: The second dimension concerns how recipients interpret the prevalence, approval, and sanctions that a normative message conveys. Lapinski et al. (2013) found that participants perceived the prevalence conveyed by each hand washing poster as intended but found the high-prevalence statistic less believable. Liu and Lapinski (2025) found that stating sanctions explicitly raised perceived injunctive norms only among participants who preferred low-context communication. These studies assessed the manipulated norms as understood by participants, as Rimal and Lapinski (2015) urged, but did not observe how that understanding is reached.
p25: The third dimension treats communication as a condition of normative influence. The TNSB specifies moderators of the descriptive norm–behavior relationship (Rimal & Real, 2005), and Lapinski and Rimal (2005) added behavioral attributes such as privacy. Privacy is a communicative condition: when a behavior cannot be known to others “either by observation or by communication about the behavior,” neither prevalence information nor sanctions can circulate (Lapinski & Rimal, 2005, p. 141). In the field, the data were not consistent with the predicted interaction between messages and privacy (Lapinski et al., 2013). Interpersonal discussion has also been treated as a moderator: descriptive norms predicted drinking more strongly among students who had discussed alcohol (Real & Rimal, 2007, as cited in Chung & Rimal, 2016).
p26a: The fourth dimension is where the critique has the most purchase. Although collective norms are defined as emerging through interaction, the formation and change of norms within a group have rarely been measured in this set of studies.
p26b: The gap lies less in theorizing (Lapinski & Rimal, 2005; Rimal & Lapinski, 2015) than in testing, because measurement has followed the TNSB, which does not specify how normative information is communicated.
p28: Chung and Rimal (2016) observed that communication scholars tend to focus on the communicative processes that lead to perceived norms, whereas social psychologists tend to emphasize how norms affect behavior. First, the field has supplied conceptual explication, distinguishing collective from perceived norms and descriptive, injunctive, and subjective norms from one another and specifying behavioral attributes such as privacy and ambiguity (Lapinski & Rimal, 2005; Park & Smith, 2007; Rimal & Lapinski, 2015). Second, it has theorized the relational variables through which norms operate: the referent group, identification with that group, and communication among its members (Rimal & Real, 2003, 2005). Third, it has treated recipients’ perception of the message as data, checking whether recipients perceived the intended norm, believed it, and inferred sanctions (Lapinski et al., 2007, 2013; Liu & Lapinski, 2025). By contrast, field experiments in psychology have evaluated norms through behavior, such as littering or energy use (Cialdini et al., 1990; Schultz et al., 2007), and in Cialdini et al.’s experiments “whether normative perceptions or some other variable was manipulated was not clear” (Lapinski et al., 2013, p. 23). Fourth, it has treated culture as a feature of communication, as in the moderating role of preferences for implicit versus explicit communication (Liu & Lapinski, 2025).
p30: The gaps can be stated in terms of the four dimensions. With respect to the channel, peer communication has been measured cross-sectionally and as frequency rather than content, so that peer selection and reverse causation (Rimal & Real, 2003) cannot be ruled out. With respect to interpretation, how recipients infer sanctions that a message leaves implied, and whether it matters who would impose them (Douglas et al., 2024), remain unexamined. With respect to change, collective norms are seldom measured, and Rimal and Lapinski (2015) found no evidence that interventions had changed injunctive or collective norms. With respect to culture, research has been concentrated in the United States (Shulman et al., 2017), and cultural processes have been proposed more often than tested directly.
p32: The first idea addresses the interpersonal channel with a three-wave panel of first-year college students, beginning at orientation, before students join new social networks (Rimal & Real, 2005). At each wave, participants would report talk about drinking by partner, frequency, and content (i.e., how much others drink vs. whether others approve), perceived norms for those partners, and their own drinking. Residence hall floor averages of drinking would serve as collective norms (Rimal & Lapinski, 2015), and random-intercept cross-lagged models would separate within-person change from stable differences (Hamaker et al., 2015).⟦FN6⟧ It is predicted that talk about how much peers drink will be positively associated with subsequent perceived descriptive norms and that talk will strengthen the association between collective and perceived descriptive norms. A panel clarifies temporal order rather than causation.
p33: The second idea addresses interpretation with an online experiment that crosses sanction (implied vs. explicit) with source (fellow members of the referent group vs. the larger community) in an injunctive norm appeal. Pressure to conform is greater when norms come from close rather than distal others (Chung & Rimal, 2016). To measure the inference of sanctions, recipients would describe in an open-ended item what would follow a violation and from whom, and then rate the likelihood of specific sanctions from each source. It is predicted that explicit sanctions will increase perceived sanctions relative to implied sanctions, especially when attributed to fellow members of the referent group. Because explicitness distinguishes low- from high-context messages (Liu & Lapinski, 2025), presenting the same messages in countries that vary in context preference would test whether culture alters injunctive appeals through the inference of implied sanctions.
p34: The third idea addresses interpretation as a process. Scalable normative feedback is one-directional, so the interpersonal discussion through which misperceptions are thought to arise (Lapinski & Rimal, 2005) is absent from their correction. Students who overestimate peer drinking would receive identical statistics through a static report or a chatbot based on a large language model, and conversation logs would be coded for the objections recipients raise and the explanations they accept.
p36: The critique does not fit an account that has located norms in communication from its first formulation. Communication has been centered least in the formation and change of norms, and culture has been treated more often as a sample characteristic than as a process; the three ideas proposed here are designed to measure these processes.
